Program:

double[] p = {0.2, 0.5, 0.3};
int[] freq = new int[3];
for (int t = 0; t < 10; t++) {
    double r = Math.random();
    double sum = 0.0;
    int j = 0;
    while (r >= sum + p[j]) {
        sum += p[j];
        j++;
    }
    freq[j]++;
}
System.out.println(freq[1]);

the rest run once, after it. | | mis:loop_body->ComputerFillsInIntent | wrong rule: The computer fills in omitted steps or values that the programmer meant, e.g. REPEAT 4 [FORWARD 30] draws a square without a turn command. | right rule: The computer executes only what the code states; every needed step and value must be written. | | mis:loop_body->ForLoopPartSkipped | wrong rule: A pass of a loop may leave out one of its parts (the condition test, the body, the update, or the initialization). | right rule: Each pass of a for loop runs test, then body, then update, every time; the initialization runs once, at the start. | | mis:loop_body->IfInLoopUnchecked | wrong rule: An if inside a loop body runs its branch on every pass without testing its condition. | right rule: The if condition is tested again on every pass, with the current values, so the branch runs only on passes where it is true. | | mis:loop_body->LoopBodyAlwaysOnce | wrong rule: The loop body always runs at least once, even if the condition is false at the start. | right rule: A while or for body runs zero times when the condition is false at the start. | | mis:loop_body->LoopBodyStatementOutsideLoop | wrong rule: Some statements inside the braces of a loop body are not repeated; they run once, before or after the loop. | right rule: Every statement inside the loop braces is part of the body and runs on every pass. | | mis:loop_body->LoopCountIsStatementCount | wrong rule: The repeat count of a counted loop says how many of the body statements are executed. | right rule: The repeat count is how many times the whole body runs; every pass runs all body statements. | | mis:loop_body->LoopOutputSameEachPass | wrong rule: A loop prints the same thing on every pass; the changing loop variable does not affect what the body does. | right rule: The body uses the current value of the loop variable, so its output can differ on each pass. | | mis:loop_body->LoopRunsStatementsSeparately | wrong rule: A loop runs its first body statement all N times, then its second body statement all N times. | right rule: Each pass runs the whole body in order, so the body statements interleave: S1, S2, S1, S2, ... | | mis:loop_body->StateChangeIgnoredAcrossPasses | wrong rule: Values changed by one pass of a loop (other than the loop variable) do not affect later passes. | right rule: Each pass starts from the state left by the previous pass, so a change in one pass carries into the next ones. | | mis:loop_body->StatementAfterLoopInBody | wrong rule: A statement written after the loop is repeated with the loop body. | right rule: The body ends at the closing brace (or after its single statement); code after it runs once, after the loop ends. | | mis:loop_body->WhileStopsMidBody | wrong rule: The loop stops the moment the condition becomes false, even in the middle of the body. | right rule: The condition is tested only before each pass, so the whole body finishes before the loop can stop. |

Edges offered: | edge | |---| | mis:control_flow->CodeAfterIfSkipped | wrong rule: When the then branch runs, the code after the if is skipped. | right rule: After the if finishes, execution continues with the next statement either way. | | mis:control_flow->FalseConditionRestartsProgram | wrong rule: When an if condition is false (and there is no else), control jumps back to the start of the program. | right rule: A false condition skips the then branch and execution continues with the statement after the if statement. | | mis:control_flow->FalseLoopRepeatsNextCode | wrong rule: A loop is an iterative if-else: while the condition is true the body repeats, and when it is false the code after the loop repeats. | right rule: Only the body is repeated; once the condition is false the code after the loop runs once. | | mis:control_flow->IfConditionWatched | wrong rule: An if statement watches its condition while the program runs and fires as soon as the condition becomes true (if = whenever). | right rule: An if condition is tested once, when control reaches the if statement; later changes to the variables do not trigger the branch. | | mis:control_flow->IfWaitsForCondition | wrong rule: An IF statement earlier in the program stays active and fires later, e.g. inside a later loop, when its condition becomes true. | right rule: An if is evaluated once when control reaches it; afterwards it is inactive unless control returns to it. | | mis:control_flow->LoopImpliedByOneTest | wrong rule: Testing one case is enough; Java will repeat the test for the other values by itself. | right rule: A statement runs once each time control reaches it; repeating a test for many values needs a loop. | | mis:control_flow->NoShortCircuit | wrong rule: logical AND/OR always evaluate both sides (Java short-circuits them) | right rule: In p && q, q is evaluated only when p is true; in p || q, q is evaluated only when p is false. | | mis:control_flow->ProgramEndsAfterLoop | wrong rule: When a loop finishes the program ends, so code after the loop never runs. | right rule: When the loop condition becomes false, control continues with the first statement after the loop. | | mis:control_flow->ProgramLooksAhead | wrong rule: The program knows or sees what later lines will do and acts on those goals at the current line, e.g. it stops 'at ten' because it wants to draw a box. | right rule: Each statement executes using only the current state; later lines have no effect until control reaches them. | | mis:control_flow->ReturnDoesNotExitLoop | wrong rule: A return inside a loop does not end the loop; it sets a value each pass (the last one is returned) or returns several values. | right rule: When return executes, the method ends at once, so the loop stops on that pass. | | mis:control_flow->StatementsRunInAnyOrder | wrong rule: Statements in a program can run in any order. | right rule: Without control statements, statements run once each, top to bottom. |
